# m21-l01 narration (generated from the outline; do not edit)

## Slide 1

Changing Magnetic Fields.

Electromagnetic induction is the process of generating current through a wire in a circuit in a changing magnetic field.

Our big question for this lesson: how can a magnet generate a current? After Oersted showed that a current makes a magnetic field, Michael Faraday was convinced the reverse must work too. In 1822 he wrote his goal in his notebook: "Convert magnetism into electricity." After about ten years of failed experiments, he did it! He induced a current in a circuit by moving a wire through a magnetic field.

That same year in America, Joseph Henry, a high school teacher who later became the first secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, made the same discovery. Figure 1 shows a modern version of their experiment. Move the wire up, and the meter swings one way. Move it down, and it swings the other way. Stop moving, and the current stops.

## Slide 3

Relative Motion.

Current is induced when a wire cuts magnetic field lines, whether the wire moves, the magnet moves, or the field changes strength.

A current can be generated in a wire in a circuit when at least part of the wire moves through, and cuts, magnetic field lines. That can happen in three ways.

First, a piece of wire can move through a field that stays still, like the wire in Figure 1. Second, a magnetic field can move past a wire that stays still. Third, the strength of the magnetic field around the wire can change. Any of these is electromagnetic induction: generating current in a circuit with a changing magnetic field.

## Slide 4

Electromotive Force.

Electromotive force, or EMF, is the potential difference that drives current in a circuit; it is a potential difference, not a force.

How does induction produce current? A current needs a source of electrical energy, like a battery. A battery keeps a potential difference in the circuit, and charges flow from higher to lower potential. The potential difference across a battery's terminals is called the electromotive force, or EMF. Despite the name, EMF is a potential difference, not a force. Like many old terms, it was named before scientists fully understood it.

You don't need a battery's chemical reaction to make an EMF. When a wire moves perpendicular to a magnetic field, the field pushes on the charges in the wire. Negative charges are pushed to one end, leaving positive charges at the other. That separation of charge creates an electric field, and so a potential difference along the wire. This is called the induced electromotive force, or induced EMF.

## Slide 5

Calculating Induced EMF.

Induced EMF in a moving wire is EMF equals B L v times the sine of theta.

How big is the induced EMF? It depends on the magnetic field strength B, the length of wire in the field L, and the part of the wire's velocity that's perpendicular to the field, v times the sine of theta. So EMF equals B times L times v times the sine of theta.

When the wire moves perpendicular to the field, the sine of ninety degrees is one, so EMF equals B L v. And when the wire moves parallel to the field, the sine of zero degrees is zero, so no EMF is induced.

Why is EMF measured in volts, like a battery? Magnetic field B is measured in teslas, and since B equals F over I L, a tesla is a newton per ampere-meter. Multiply newtons per ampere-meter by meters by meters per second, and you get newton-meters per ampere-second. A newton-meter is a joule and an ampere-second is a coulomb, and a joule per coulomb is a volt. If the wire is part of a circuit with resistance R, the current is I equals EMF divided by R.

## Slide 6

Direction of the Induced Current.

Thumb along the wire's motion, fingers along the field, and your right palm points in the direction of the induced current.

Which way does the induced current flow? As the wire moves through the field, the field pushes on the charges in the wire, and they move in the direction of that force, as in the top of Figure 2.

Find that direction with the right-hand rule in the bottom of Figure 2. Point your thumb in the direction the wire moves and your fingers in the direction of the magnetic field. Your palm points in the direction of the force on positive charges, and that's the direction of the current.

## Slide 7

Example Problem 1, Induced EMF.

For a wire moving perpendicular to a field, EMF equals B L v, and I equals EMF divided by R.

A straight wire is part of a circuit with a resistance of 0.50 ohms. The wire is 0.20 meters long and moves at a steady 7.0 meters per second perpendicular to a magnetic field of 8.0 times ten to the negative second teslas. What EMF is induced? What's the current? And if a different metal raised the resistance to 0.78 ohms, what would the new current be?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Draw the wire of length L and close the circuit with an ammeter. Show the field B perpendicular to the wire, and the velocity v perpendicular to both. Use the right-hand rule to find the current's direction. Known: v is 7.0 meters per second, L is 0.20 meters, B is 8.0 times ten to the negative second teslas, R one is 0.50 ohms, and R two is 0.78 ohms. Unknown: EMF and I.

Step two: solve. EMF equals B L v: 8.0 times ten to the negative second teslas, times 0.20 meters, times 7.0 meters per second, is 0.11 tesla square meters per second, or 0.11 volts. The current is EMF over R: 0.11 volts divided by 0.50 ohms is 0.22 amperes. With 0.78 ohms, it's 0.11 volts divided by 0.78 ohms, or 0.14 amperes. The current flows counterclockwise.

Step three: evaluate. Volts is the right unit for EMF, and amperes for current. The direction follows the right-hand rule: v along the thumb, B along the fingers, and the force out of the palm, with current in the same direction as the force. And currents around a tenth of an ampere are typical for circuits with small EMFs and resistances.

## Slide 8

Induced EMF in Microphones.

A microphone converts sound into electrical signals by electromagnetic induction.

Remember how earbuds use magnetic forces to make sound? Microphones are built the same way but work in reverse. They turn sound into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction.

A microphone has a thin aluminum diaphragm attached to a coil in a magnetic field, as in Figure 3. Sound waves make the diaphragm vibrate, which moves the coil. The coil moving in the magnetic field induces an EMF across its ends, which drives a current. The EMF and current change with the sound, so the sound wave becomes an electrical signal. These potential differences are tiny, typically about ten to the negative third volts, but electronic devices can amplify them.

Love music and have a great ear? Audio engineers shape how recordings sound by choosing microphones, setting levels, and adjusting the sound.

## Slide 9

Electric Generators.

An electric generator converts mechanical energy to electrical energy.

Microphones are just one use of electromagnetic induction. It's also how electric generators work. An electric generator converts mechanical energy to electrical energy. It has many wire loops in a magnetic field, wound around an iron core that concentrates the magnetic flux through the wire. The iron and wire together make up the generator's armature, also called a rotor.

Like a motor's armature, a generator's armature can spin freely in a magnetic field. As it turns, its loops cut through magnetic field lines, inducing an EMF in each loop. Since EMF depends on wire length, field strength, and speed, more loops mean more wire and a bigger total EMF. And a bigger EMF drives a stronger current.

## Slide 10

Orientation of the Loop.

A rotating loop's induced current is greatest when its sides move perpendicular to the field and zero when they move parallel to it.

To see how a generator makes current, look at the single loop in Figure 4. It sits in a magnetic field and is part of a closed circuit, so the induced EMF drives a current. As the loop spins, the strength and direction of the current change, because the direction of the loop's motion relative to the field keeps changing.

Only the part of the wire's velocity perpendicular to the field induces an EMF. So the current is strongest when the loop's sides move straight across the field, which happens when the loop is horizontal, as in Figure 4 and the far left of Figure 5.

As the loop turns toward vertical, its sides move through the field lines at a smaller and smaller angle, cutting fewer lines each second, so the current drops. When the loop is vertical, as in the middle of Figure 5, the sides move parallel to the field, and the current is zero.

## Slide 11

Current Reversals and Where Current Is Induced.

A generator loop's current varies sinusoidally and reverses every half-turn.

Keep the loop spinning, and the current rises smoothly from zero to a maximum and back to zero every half-turn. Each time the loop turns through 180 degrees, the current reverses. The graph at the far right of Figure 5 shows this smooth, wavelike pattern, called sinusoidal.

Not every part of the loop helps. In Figure 6, only two sides contribute an EMF. Apply the right-hand rule to the long segment ab, and the force on the charges points across the wire, not along it, so no current is driven along it. The same goes for segment cd. But in segment bc the current flows from b to c, and in segment ad it flows from d to a.

So in the equation EMF equals B L v times the sine of theta, L is the combined length of segments ad and bc. The biggest potential difference is induced when those segments move perpendicular to the field, when theta is ninety degrees, which is when the loop is horizontal, lying along the field.

## Slide 12

Sources of Mechanical Energy.

Generators and motors are built almost the same way but convert energy in opposite directions.

Real generators, like those in wind turbines, have many loops in their armatures, but they make current just like a single loop. Wind spins the turbine blades, giving them rotational kinetic energy. The blades are connected to an armature in a magnetic field, so as the armature turns, an EMF is induced in each loop. Connect the generator to a circuit, and current flows.

Generators and electric motors are built almost the same way, but they convert energy in opposite directions. A generator turns mechanical energy into electrical energy, and a motor turns electrical energy into mechanical energy.

Power-plant generators are traditionally turned by steam from water heated by burning fossil fuels or by fissioning uranium. Wind and moving water can turn them too. The generators at the Hoover Dam in Figure 7, on the Nevada-Arizona border, convert the energy of falling water into electrical energy.

## Slide 13

AC and DC Generators.

Alternating current, or AC, reverses direction at a fixed rate; direct current, or DC, moves in one direction.

There are two main types of generators. In direct current, or DC, generators, charges move in one direction, just as they do with batteries. The armature connects to the circuit through a commutator, which keeps the current flowing one way.

Alternating current, or AC, generators connect to the circuit with slip rings instead. One ring connects to one end of the armature, and the other ring to the other end, as in the left of Figure 8. Every 180 degrees of rotation, the induced EMF reverses, so the current reverses too. In a generator turning steadily, the current alternates at a fixed rate and varies sinusoidally, as in the top graph of Figure 8. The current is zero when the armature's loop is vertical, perpendicular to the field, with its sides moving parallel to the field lines.

In the United States, utilities use 60 hertz: the current goes one way, then the other, and back, 60 times every second. In a simple two-pole generator like this one, that means 60 complete rotations each second. Many other countries use 50 hertz.

## Slide 14

Average Power and Effective Current.

Effective current is the square root of two over two times the maximum current, or 0.707 times I max.

An AC generator's power is current times potential difference, and since both keep changing, so does the power. The bottom graph of Figure 8 shows power versus time. Notice it's always positive, because I and V are always both positive or both negative together. The average power is half the maximum power: P AC equals one half P AC max.

We usually describe AC with effective values instead of maximum values. Since P equals the square of I times R, the effective current is defined by P AC equals the square of I eff, times R. Start with P AC equals one half P AC max, substitute the square of I times R on each side, and solve. You get I eff equals the square root of two over two, times I max, which is 0.707 times I max.

## Slide 15

Effective Potential Difference and the War of Currents.

Effective, or RMS, potential difference is 0.707 times the maximum potential difference.

The same idea works for voltage. Since P equals the square of V divided by R, the effective potential difference is V eff equals the square root of two over two, times V max, or 0.707 times V max. Effective potential difference is often called RMS, for root mean square, potential difference. In the United States, wall outlets are described as 120 volts RMS. In many other countries, it's 240 volts RMS.

Here's a bit of history. Thomas Edison built the first electrical distribution system in the United States in the late 1800s, and it used direct current. Soon Nikola Tesla developed a competing system using alternating current, and he teamed up with George Westinghouse to promote it. A "war of the currents" followed. In the end, AC won. You'll find out why in the next lesson.
